ety.text: From Middle English toll, tol, tolle, from Old English toll m or n and toln f (“toll, duty, custom”), from Proto-West Germanic *toll, *tolnu, from Proto-Germanic *tullaz, *tullō (“that which is counted or told, reckoning”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“calculation, fraud”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Tol (“toll”), Dutch tol (“toll”), German Zoll (“toll, duty, customs”), Danish told (“toll, duty, tariff”), Swedish tull (“toll, customs”), Icelandic tollur (“toll, customs”). More at tell, tale.
Probably the same as Etymology 3. Possibly related to or influenced by toil

From Middle English tolen, tollen, variation of tullen, tillen (“to draw, allure, entice”), from Old English *tyllan, *tillan (“to pull, draw, attract”) (found in compounds fortyllan (“to seduce, lead astray, draw away from the mark, deceive”) and betyllan, betillan (“to lure, decoy”)), related to Old Frisian tilla (“to lift, raise”), Dutch tillen (“to lift, raise, weigh, buy”), Low German tillen (“to lift, remove”), Swedish dialectal tille (“to take up, appropriate”).
From Latin tollō (“to lift up”).

senses.d: A fee paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for the privilege of passing over a bridge or on a highway, or for that of vending goods in a fair, market, etc.
Loss or damage incurred through a disaster.
ex: The war has taken its toll on the people.

senses.d: A fee paid by the owner of materials or other goods for processing such goods, as under a tolling agreement.
ex: toll ore refining; toll manufacturing

senses.d: A fee for using any kind of material processing service.
ex: We can handle on a toll basis your needs for spray drying, repackaging, crushing and grinding, and dry blending.

senses.d: A tollbooth.
ex: We will be replacing some manned tolls with high-speed device readers.

senses.d: A liberty to buy and sell within the bounds of a manor.
A portion of grain taken by a miller as a compensation for grinding.
To impose a fee for the use of.
ex: Once more it is proposed to toll the East River bridges.

senses.d: To levy a toll on (someone or something).
ex:
No Italian priest
Shall tithe or toll in our dominions.

senses.d: To take as a toll.
To pay a toll or tallage.
ex: I will buy me a sonne in Law in a faire, and toule for this. Ile none of him.

senses.d: The act or sound of ringing a bell, especially slowly, as with a church or cemetery bell.
To ring (a bell) slowly and repeatedly.
ex: Martin tolled the great bell every day.
Ask not for whom the bell tolls.

senses.d: To summon by ringing a bell.
ex: The ringer tolled the workers back from the fields for vespers.

When hollow murmurs of their evening bells
Dismiss the sleepy swains, and toll them to their cells.

senses.d: To announce by ringing a bell.
ex: The bells tolled the King’s death.

senses.d: To make a sound as if made by a bell.
ex: The chaplain's first mention of the name Yossarian! had tolled deep in his memory like a portentous gong.

senses.d: To draw; pull; tug; drag.
To tear in pieces.
To draw; entice; invite; allure.
ex: Hou many virgins shal she tolle and drawe to þe Lord - "Life of Our Lady"

senses.d: To lure with bait; tole (especially, fish and animals).
To take away; to vacate; to annul.
To suspend.
ex: The statute of limitations defense was tolled as a result of the defendant’s wrongful conduct.

ety.text: Via Provençal pezatge, from Medieval Latin pedāticum (found in medieval charters), from Latin pedem (“foot”). Alternatively a very old derivation of Old French pied (cf. the medieval forms paage, peage). Unrelated to the verb payer (“to pay”).
From Old French peage or Old Occitan pezatge, both from Medieval Latin pedāticum, derived from Latin pes (“foot”). Modelled in Italian after piede + -aggio.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin datium, by-form of Medieval Latin dātiō (“the act of giving”).

ex: The party tolerated corruption within its ranks.

senses.d: To bear, withstand.

ety.text: Either borrowed from French tolérant or directly from its source Latin tolerans, present participle of, and participial adjective from tolerō (“to endure”).

senses.d: Tending to permit, allow, understand, or accept something.
ex: He's pretty tolerant of different political views, but don't ask him about religion.

senses.d: Tending to withstand or survive.
ex: These plants are tolerant of drought and sunlight.

senses.d: One who or that which tolerates something, especially a biological species.

grp.label: tending to permit, allow, understand, or accept something

pt:tolerante.gl: tolerant (tending to permit, allow, understand, or accept something)

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English toleraunce, borrowed from Old French tolerance, from Latin tolerantia (“endurance”), from tolerāns, present participle of, and participial adjective from Latin tolerō (“to endure”).

senses.d: The ability to endure pain or hardship; endurance.
The ability or practice of tolerating; an acceptance of or patience with the beliefs, opinions or practices of others; a lack of bigotry.
ex: Near-synonym: forbearance

senses.d: The ability of the body (or other organism) to resist the action of a poison, to cope with a dangerous drug or to survive infection by an organism.
Resistance to drunkenness.
ex: Since he hadn't had any alcohol in years, his tolerance was very low, and it only took two drinks for him to get sloshed.

senses.d: The variation or deviation from a standard, especially the maximum permitted variation in an engineering measurement.
ex: Our customers can generally accept ten times the tolerance which we can achieve in our machining operations.

senses.d: The ability of the body to accept a tissue graft without rejection.
To design or engineer a material to a specified tolerance.
